Yes. One geometry-based optimizer, ArcGD, was tested on a highly non-convex Rosenbrock function and consistently outperformed Adam under one matched-learning-rate setting, while achieving superior final solutions in most cases under the other setting [1]. Another geometry-focused method, Muon, also improved over Adam on equivariant and molecular settings, and it was reported to substantially outperform Adam in interatomic-potential training [2, 4].

The papers do not show that geometry-based optimizers always beat Adam on all non-convex surfaces. They show improvements in specific non-convex benchmarks and training tasks, while other work focuses on explaining Adam’s behavior or conditions for its convergence rather than proving it is generally worse [7, 9, 10].
